narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ovid’s Roman epic, Theseus abandons Ariadne after the escape from Crete. Liber helps the deserted woman and sets her crown among the stars. Transformation moves the narrative beyond the hero’s successful escape.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “the son of Ægeus, carrying away the daughter of Minos, sets sail for Dia,[13] and barbarously deserts his companion on those shores. Her, {thus} deserted and greatly lamenting, Liber embraces and aids; and, that she may be famed by a lasting Constellation, he places in the heavens the crown taken from”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: Reception is evidence twice over: it preserves material and shows how a later culture chose to reorganize it.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Distinguish Ovid’s narrative from Riley’s explanatory summaries and footnotes in the same volume. Compare the thread, abandonment, and crown across named works instead of importing Ovid into every Greek version.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Later storytelling is part of mythology, but it must stay labeled as later storytelling.

quiz.prompt: Why label Ovid as Roman reception here?

choices.text: His later Latin epic reshapes material also found in Greek traditions.
He is the Greek eyewitness who built the labyrinth.
